fatal_errors: The hypothesis assumes a single-phase alloy, whereas the target material is an 83% FCC/17% BCC nanocrystalline alloy.
It replaces the governing HEBM-SPS processing comparison with compositional substitution and therefore does not reconstruct the target intervention or process window.

It attributes strength predominantly to atomic-size lattice distortion while omitting the target's principal coupled mediators: nanocrystalline grain size, milling-induced dislocation density, densification, and reduced porosity.
Composition substitutions cannot vary atomic-size mismatch independently of elastic modulus, stacking-fault energy, chemical ordering, and phase stability, weakening causal attribution.
explanation: The proposal is scientifically plausible as a generic solid-solution-strengthening hypothesis for single-phase HEAs and includes a baseline, boundaries, measurements, and an explicit falsification rule. It nevertheless has little agreement with the hidden target. The target concerns nominally equimolar CoCrFeNiTi powders subjected to 1–6 h high-energy ball milling and 900–1000°C spark-plasma sintering, with strength governed synergistically by nanocrystalline Hall–Petch strengthening, accumulated defects, solid-solution effects, densification, and a stabilized FCC/BCC mixture. The generated hypothesis instead varies chemistry and predicts only an unspecified positive hardness/strength trend, without reconstructing the reported phase fractions, sub-48 nm grains, 675 Hv hardness, 1894 MPa compressive strength, or cast-alloy baseline. Its experiment is directionally discriminating but XRD line broadening is not unique evidence of atomic-size distortion because crystallite size and dislocation microstrain also broaden peaks. No cited evidence supports the asserted predominance of lattice distortion.
